framed_question: How can the hyperscript skill be improved? What's missing, weak, redundant, or could be better structured? Consider: clarity, completeness, triggering accuracy, examples, edge cases, anti-patterns, organization, and real-world effectiveness.

advisors.name: The Contrarian
advisors.response:
This skill has a fundamental structural problem: it's a reference document pretending to be a skill. The SKILL.md itself is 90% routing table and 10% actual guidance. The 'Critical Rules' section is the only genuinely valuable part because it tells you what TO DO and what NOT TO do. Everything else is 'go read this other file' — which is fine for a knowledge base but mediocre for a skill.

The 'When NOT to Use Hyperscript' section is weak. Rule 3 says 'if the solution would be mostly js ... end blocks, skip hyperscript' — but where's the threshold? 50%? 80%? An agent will hit a case that's 40% JS interop and have no idea what to do. Give concrete heuristics or an example.

The setup essentials section burbs the `_hyperscript.browserInit()` call inside a build/import subsection. That's a critical step that deserves its own callout for npm/bundler users, because forgetting it is the #1 gotcha.

The HTMX Companion section is the best part of this skill but it's too short. The single example `on htmx:beforeRequest add @disabled then on htmx:afterRequest remove @disabled` is the most common pattern — and it's buried in the middle of a paragraph. This should be prominent, with at least 3 more real-world HTMX+hyperscript patterns.

The description trigger says 'whenever the user is building, debugging, or reviewing hyperscript code' but the skill itself barely covers debugging at all. There's zero troubleshooting guidance. What are the common errors? What does a parse failure look like? How do you debug a handler that fires but does the wrong thing? This is a glaring omission.

Finally, the `target_versions` field says 0.9.x but `last_verified` is April 2026. The version pinning in the CDN example is 0.9.14. What if 0.9.15 changes something? The skill should advise checking the current version rather than hardcoding a specific one, or at minimum explain when to update the pinned version.

advisors.name: The First Principles Thinker
advisors.response:
What is hyperscript actually for? It's an event-driven, element-scoped scripting language that lets you write behavioral logic directly on DOM nodes without a build step. That's the core value proposition. Every structural decision in this skill should flow from that.

Currently the skill organizes information by technical category (syntax, DOM, events, advanced). But the user's mental model isn't organized that way — it's organized by task: 'I want this button to do X when clicked,' 'I want to show a loading state,' 'I want to validate this form.' The reference map at the bottom is accurate but it's a lookup table, not a task guide.

The Quick Start section attempts task orientation but collapses into 'identify the domain → open reference file → implement → validate.' That's a generic process, not hyperscript-specific guidance. What would actually help: start with the most common hyperscript tasks users actually face, and for each one, show the minimal pattern.

The Critical Rules section is closest to first-prices thinking because it captures invariants — things that are always true regardless of the specific task. These rules are load-bearing. Rule about math parenthesization alone will save hours of debugging. Rule about attribute storage being string-based is equally important. But Rule 5 about JS interop is mushy: 'use js ... end for cases where hyperscript genuinely cannot express the logic.' That's circular. What CAN'T hyperscript express? Tell me concretely: complex algorithmic logic, external library calls, anything requiring precise type coercion beyond the built-in conversions.

The reference files are treated as opaque black boxes in the SKILL.md. The skill should extract the single most important gotcha from each reference file and surface it inline. If I'm looking at dom-and-commands.md, what's the one thing that will bite me? The skill should tell me upfront.

advisors.name: The Expansionist
advisors.response:
This skill massively undersells hyperscript by framing it as 'event handlers and DOM glue.' That's the minimum viable pitch, but hyperscript can do much more — and the skill should showcase that power.

First, behaviors are barely covered. The `behavior` keyword is one of hyperscript's most distinctive features: reusable, named behavioral mixins that you install on elements. This is a powerful abstraction that no other front-end tool offers in quite the same way. The SKILL.md mentions behaviors exactly once in Critical Rules #9 and once in the reference map. There should be a dedicated section showing how to define and install behaviors, with at least two examples: a simple one (auto-focusing an input) and a composable one (a toggle group).

Second, the `worker` feature is mentioned only as a footnote about separate bundles. Web workers are genuinely useful for offloading computation without leaving the hyperscript mental model. A real example — like performing a calculation in a worker and updating the DOM on completion — would make this skill dramatically more useful.

Third, hyperscript's string-based templating with `put`, `set`, and `fetch` is practically a mini reactive framework. The skill could show a pattern where an element fetches HTML, puts it into the DOM, and adds event handlers — all without leaving hyperscript. This is the kind of example that makes someone say 'I didn't know it could do that.'

Fourth, the HTMX integration section should be expanded to show a full request lifecycle: click handler → disable button → add loading class → htmx request fires → hyperscript handles afterSwap → remove loading class → re-enable button → show toast notification. This end-to-end pattern is what real applications need.

Fifth, the skill should have a 'Common Patterns' section with copy-pasteable snippets for: accordion toggle, tab group, form validation feedback, modal open/close, and optimistic UI updates. These are the patterns that prove hyperscript's value in practice.

advisors.name: The Outsider
advisors.response:
I've never heard of hyperscript before reading this skill. Here's what confused me:

The very first thing I see after the frontmatter is 'Quick Start' which tells me to 'identify the domain of the task' and 'open the matching file from references/.' I don't know what the domains are. I don't know what's in those reference files. This is telling me to look things up before I even understand what the tool does.

The description uses terms like 'natural-language command syntax' and 'localized DOM/event behavior' without explaining what those mean in practice. Show me what hyperserscript code looks like in the first 30 seconds. I need a concrete 'before/after' — show me the plain JS version and the hyperscript version side by side so I can see the difference.

The 'Setup Essentials' section has a code block labeled 'CDN install' and another 'Build/import.' I don't know which one I need. A beginner doesn't know the difference between a CDN install and a build/import. Just tell me: if you're adding this to an HTML file, use this; if you're using npm/webpack/vite, use this. Don't make me figure out the category.

Critical Rules #2 about queue semantics lists five options. I have no idea what 'queue last' means versus 'queue none.' An example would help: 'If a user clicks a button three times rapidly and the handler makes an HTTP request, queue last means only the third click fires.' Without concrete scenarios, these are just words.

The skill mentions `processNode()` twice but never shows me what 'dynamically inserted DOM' looks like. When would I be inserting DOM manually? I might not even know I need this function. A code example showing the problem (innerHTML assignment that doesn't trigger hyperscript) would make this click instantly.

Finally, the HTMX Companion section is the part I understand best because it relates to something I might actually do (disable buttons during requests). But the section heading says 'Guidance' and then the content is mostly telling me what NOT to do. Give me a clear DO section with working code.

advisors.name: The Executor
advisors.response:
The highest-impact improvement is also the simplest: add a 'Debugging & Troubleshooting' section. Right now there's zero debugging guidance. Every user will eventually hit a handler that doesn't fire, fires twice, or throws a cryptic parse error. The skill must answer: what does a hyperscript error look like in the console? How do you inspect the compiled behavior? What are the top 5 parse errors and their fixes? This is the single biggest gap.

Second: create a 'Patterns' section with 5-8 copy-pasteable code examples for the most common use cases. Not links to reference files — actual inline code. The patterns should be: (1) click toggle, (2) disable button during HTMX request, (3) show/hide with transition, (4) fetch and render, (5) form validation feedback. Drop-in code that works. This alone would make the skill 3x more useful.

Third: fix the CDN version pinning. Change the hardcoded `@0.9.14` to a note that says 'pin the latest 0.9.x version for production; check the hyperscript releases page for current.' Stale version pins in skills erode trust.

Fourth: the 'When NOT to Use' section needs one concrete example per bullet. Not abstract advice — a code snippet that shows the anti-pattern. Show me the hyperscript code that's doing too much, then show me the JavaScript replacement. That's how an agent learns to recognize the boundary.

These four changes take maybe 2 hours to implement and would close the skill's biggest gaps. Everything else — expanded behaviors coverage, worker examples, pattern libraries — is phase two. Start with debugging and patterns. Those are the things that prevent real failures.

peer_reviews.strongest: The Executor. The debugging section recommendation is the highest-leverage fix — it addresses a gap that causes real pain for every hyperscript user, and it's specific, actionable, and fast to implement. The patterns section with inline copy-pasteable code would transform the skill from a lookup table into something genuinely useful at the moment of implementation.
peer_reviews.biggest_blind_spot: The Contrarian. Much of the criticism is valid but the response reads a bit like 'this reference model is wrong' without acknowledging that skills in this repo are explicitly designed to delegate to reference files. The reference-file architecture is a deliberate pattern across the repo. Criticizing the skill for following the established pattern is fair, but the Contrarian doesn't acknowledge that consistency with other skills (django, htmx) has its own value.
peer_reviews.what_all_missed: Nobody addressed the eval file. There's an evals.json that presumably tests this skill — nobody asked whether the evals are any good, whether they cover the common failure modes, or whether they need updating alongside any skill changes. Also, nobody mentioned the evals when discussing what patterns the skill should cover. If the evals are sparse or test the wrong things, the skill has no feedback loop.

peer_reviews.strongest: The Expansionist. The point about behaviors being massively undercovered hits hard. Behaviors are arguably hyperscript's killer feature for real applications — reusable behavioral mixins are a genuinely unique abstraction. The suggestion to show a full HTMX lifecycle pattern (disable → loading → swap → toast) is the kind of end-to-end example that turns a reference doc into a practical skill. The Executor's patterns section is close but the Expansionist goes further by identifying WHERE the unique value is.
peer_reviews.biggest_blind_spot: The Outsider. While the outsider perspective is useful, most of the confusion points are about things that any hyperscript user would face on first encounter — that's expected for a skill that presumably gets loaded when the user is already working with hyperscript. The real outsider concern should be: does the description trigger correctly? And nobody, including the Outsider, deeply analyzed the description's triggering accuracy.
peer_reviews.what_all_missed: The description's scope claim and the actual skill coverage don't match. The description mentions 'worker' and 'socket' and 'eventsource' as triggers, but the SKILL.md explicitly says these require separate bundles and barely covers them. So the description promises coverage the skill can't deliver. Nobody flagged this trigger-to-content mismatch, which is a real problem — an agent will load this skill for worker-specific questions and find almost nothing useful.

peer_reviews.strongest: The Executor, specifically the point about anti-patterns and inline examples. The Executor correctly identifies that the 'When NOT to Use' section is the weakest structural element — it gives abstract warnings without showing what the wrong approach looks like. A side-by-side comparison (bad hyperscript vs. good JavaScript) would make each bullet immediately actionable. The Executor focuses on what prevents real-world failures, which is exactly what a skill should do.
peer_reviews.biggest_blind_spot: The First Principles Thinker. The suggestion to reorganize by task category instead of technical category sounds good in theory but ignores the reality that the reference files already exist and are organized by technical domain. Reorganizing the routing layer while keeping the reference files as-is would create a mismatch between the task-oriented entry points and the domain-oriented reference material. This would make the skill harder to maintain, not easier.
peer_reviews.what_all_missed: Nobody discussed the `REFERENCE.md` index file's role in this skill. The Task Routing section says 'unsure where to start → references/REFERENCE.md' but nobody evaluated whether that landing page is effective. If someone is lost, is REFERENCE.md actually helpful? Is it a good index? This is the safety net of the skill and nobody checked if it works.

peer_reviews.strongest: The Contrarian's point about the version pinning is the most concretely actionable single-issue in the entire debate. The CDN example hardcodes `@0.9.14` which will go stale. A stale version pin in a skill that ships to agents is worse than no pin at all because it creates false confidence. The fix is a one-line change. This should be the first thing fixed.
peer_reviews.biggest_blind_spot: The First Principles Thinker says 'extract the single most important gotcha from each reference file and surface it inline.' This would create maintenance nightmares — every time a reference file changes, the SKILL.md needs updating. It also bloats the SKILL.md. The whole point of the reference-file architecture is to avoid this duplication. The suggestion contradicts the repo's own design pattern documented in AGENTS.md.
peer_reviews.what_all_missed: Nobody addressed the `scope: hyperscript` frontmatter field. Other skills like django have `scope: project` — what does `scope: hyperscript` actually mean for the pi agent system? Is it a user-level or project-level skill? This ambiguity could affect when and how it gets loaded, and the skill should clarify this or the frontmatter should be corrected. Also, nobody asked whether the `htmx` skill cross-references are actually present in the htmx skill, creating a bidirectional link.

peer_reviews.strongest: The Outsider's critique of the CDN vs. build/import confusion exposes a real structural problem. The Setup Essentials section should use two clearly labeled paths: 'I have an HTML file' vs. 'I use npm/vite/webpack.' This framing matches how users actually think. The Outsider's perspective is valuable because it identifies where the skill assumes knowledge that a first-time user doesn't have. The Executor's debugging recommendation is important but the Outsider's readability fixes will impact every single skill invocation, not just the debugging ones.
peer_reviews.biggest_blind_spot: The Expansionist's enthusiasm for behaviors, workers, and end-to-end patterns is exciting but risks scope creep. The skill's description explicitly defines a focused scope (local DOM/event behavior). Adding worker examples and full reactive patterns would bloat the skill and potentially make it trigger for tasks that are better served by JavaScript. The Expansionist is effectively arguing for a different skill, not an improved version of this one.
peer_reviews.what_all_missed: Critical Rules #6 and #7 both address the same boundary — when to stop using hyperscript. Rule 6 says 'prefer local behavior, not global sprawl' and Rule 7 says 'HTMX ownership stays separate.' These overlap. Rule 6 is about architectural scope (how many elements should one piece of hyperscript touch?) while Rule 7 is about framework boundary (when does HTMX handle this instead?). They should either be merged or given clearer differentiation with an example that shows the distinction. Nobody caught this redundancy.

chairman_verdict.agrees: The council strongly agrees on three points: (1) The skill needs a debugging/troubleshooting section — this is the single biggest gap causing real user pain. (2) The skill needs concrete, copy-pasteable code examples inline in the SKILL.md, not just links to reference files. The HTMX companion example with `on htmx:beforeRequest add @disabled` is the right model but there's only one of them. (3) The 'When NOT to Use' section is ineffective as written — it needs side-by-side anti-pattern examples showing bad hyperscript and its JavaScript replacement. There is also agreement that version pinning (`@0.9.14`) is a problem, behaviors are undercovered, and the setup essentials need clearer beginner-friendly framing.
chairman_verdict.clashes: The council clashes on whether to reorganize the skill around tasks vs. keeping the technical domain structure. The First Principles Thinker and Expansionist want task-based organization with patterns and end-to-end examples baked into the top-level skill. The Contrarian and parts of the Executor suggest surgically adding specific sections without restructuring. Reviewer 3 and Reviewer 4 also pushed back on the First Principles approach, arguing it contradicts the repo's established reference-file architecture. On scope: the Expansionist wants to expand into workers, behaviors, and full reactive patterns, while Reviewer 5 warns this would bloat the skill against its defined scope. On reference-file coupling: the First Principles Thinker wants gotchas extracted inline, but Reviewer 4 argues this creates maintenance debt that contradicts the repo design pattern.
chairman_verdict.blind_spots: The evals.json file was completely ignored by all five advisors and most reviewers. Only Reviewer 1 mentioned it, noting that without good evals the skill has no feedback loop for quality. The `scope: hyperscript` frontmatter field was also unexamined — its meaning and correctness relative to other skills' scope values is unknown. Critical Rules #6 and #7 overlap without clear differentiation — nobody flagged this redundancy. The REFERENCE.md index file, which serves as the skill's 'I'm lost' landing page, was never evaluated for effectiveness. Finally, the description-to-content mismatch (description triggers on worker/socket/eventsource but the skill can't deliver on those) was only caught by Reviewer 2.
chairman_verdict.recommendation: Make three surgical changes now: (1) Add a Debugging & Troubleshooting section covering the top 5 parse errors, what errors look like in the console, and how to inspect compiled behaviors. (2) Expand the HTMX Companion section into a full Patterns section with 5-8 inline code examples covering the most common real-world tasks. (3) Rewrite each 'When NOT to Use' bullet with a concrete anti-pattern example showing the bad hyperscript version and the better alternative. Then make two structural improvements: (4) Move the CDN example's version pin to a variable/comment noting to use the latest 0.9.x, and (5) Rewrite Setup Essentials with two clear paths: 'I have an HTML file' vs. 'I use a build tool.' Do NOT reorganize the reference architecture or expand into workers/full reactivity — that's a separate skill or v2. Evaluate evals.json coverage after these changes and add eval cases for the new patterns.
chairman_verdict.first_step: Add the Debugging & Troubleshooting section. Open the reference files, identify the top 5 most common errors (parse failures, silent no-fires, queue surprises, math parenthesization, and js interop type issues), and write a concise section with each error's symptoms, cause, and fix. This is the highest-impact change because it addresses pain that every hyperscript user hits, and it requires no structural changes to the skill.
